analysis.one_liner: Requires employers with 15 or more workers to let employees earn up to seven paid sick days a year.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let workers at businesses with 15 or more employees earn up to seven paid sick days a year, never received a committee vote or a House floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Healthy Families Act would have required businesses with 15 or more employees to let workers earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to seven days (56 hours) a year. Workers could use the time for their own illness or medical care, to care for a sick child, spouse, or parent, or to handle medical, legal, and safety needs after domestic violence or stalking. Employers who already offered equivalent paid leave would not have to change anything, and the bill barred employers from firing or penalizing workers for using the time. The bill never got a vote: it sat in committee and a subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at businesses with 15 or more employees who lack paid sick time — concentrated among low-wage workers, women, and single parents, who the bill's findings say are the least likely to have it. The bill also covers time to care for sick family members, so working parents avoid losing pay or sending sick children to school and child care. Victims of domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking gain protected paid time to seek medical care, counseling, safety, or court action without risking their job.

how_it_helps.text: Every worker at a covered employer would earn at least one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours (seven days) a year, usable for their own illness, a doctor's visit, or preventive care.
The time could also be used to care for a sick child, spouse, parent, or family-equivalent relation — covering the tens of millions of workers whose existing leave, if any, covers only themselves.
Victims of domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking could use the time for medical care, counseling, relocation, or court proceedings without losing pay or their job.

The bill bans employer retaliation for using or asking for sick time, bars counting it against no-fault attendance policies, and lets workers sue for lost wages and reinstatement, with attorney's fees available.
Employers with existing paid-leave policies at least as generous and usable for the same purposes get full credit, so most workers who already have sick leave would see no change.

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers — those with 15 or more employees — pay up to 56 hours of wages per worker per year for new sick leave, plus notice, recordkeeping, and possible damages and attorney's fees if they interfere with the right. Small employers near the 15-employee threshold and labor-intensive businesses bear proportionally larger costs; employers with already-equivalent policies pay nothing.

drawbacks.text: The mandate falls on employers, who must pay for up to 56 hours of leave per worker per year plus compliance and recordkeeping costs; small businesses just above the 15-employee threshold would face the same requirements as large firms.
Employers may require doctor's certification for any sick absence longer than three consecutive workdays, which could impose costs and delays on workers without easy access to a health care provider.
The bill allows employees to sue employers for damages and attorney's fees, which opponents of such mandates typically argue invites litigation against employers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is substantial: roughly half of American workers, and about 79 percent of the lowest-earning families, lacked paid sick time when the bill was introduced, and the bill's own findings cite evidence that paid sick leave reduces disease spread, cuts emergency-room use, and protects domestic violence victims from losing their jobs. The main costs fall on employers of 15 or more workers, who would bear up to 7 paid sick days per employee per year plus compliance and recordkeeping; small firms near the 15-employee threshold and low-margin businesses would feel this most, and some employers might slow hiring or reduce other benefits in response. The bill limits these costs with a 56-hour cap, no cash-out at separation, and credit for existing generous policies, making it a moderate, not maximal, mandate. On balance it is a genuine worker benefit with real but manageable employer costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to three House committees, handed to a subcommittee four weeks later, and never got a markup or a vote before the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 18, 2009, and referred to three committees: Education and Labor, Oversight and Government Reform, and House Administration.
On June 11, 2009, the House Education and Labor Committee referred it to its Subcommittee on Workforce Protections — the last recorded action of any kind.

No further action was ever taken; the bill sat at the subcommittee stage until the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, with no committee vote, no floor vote, and no Senate companion action reflected in the record.
All 125 cosponsors were Democrats — nearly half of the Democratic caucus — but not the majority needed to move a bill through committee and floor without leadership scheduling it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of 15 or more workers, especially in low-wage industries, avoided a new paid-leave mandate of up to seven days per employee per year. Workers without paid sick time — about half of Americans, and nearly 80 percent of the lowest-earning families, by the bill's own findings — got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers; workers without sick leave gained nothing

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited the initial cosponsors.

for.name: George Miller
for.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
for.what_they_did: Original co-sponsor of the bill and chair of the committee to which it was primarily referred; the committee never reported it out.

against.name: Business and employer associations
against.role: Industry groups opposing mandated paid sick leave
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandated paid sick leave nationally, arguing it imposes payroll and compliance costs on employers; no action by these groups on this bill appears in the congressional record.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee markup or a floor vote despite a large Democratic majority and 125 cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: All 125 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican support appears in the record; the bill died in a Democratically controlled committee without a vote.

industries.industry: Employers of low-wage hourly workers (retail, food service, hospitality, child care)
industries.note: These employers would bear the cost of up to seven paid sick days per worker per year — a cost they currently avoid because their workers are the least likely to have paid sick leave. The bill caps the cost at 56 hours a year and credits employers who already offer comparable leave.

industries.industry: Small businesses with 15 or more employees
industries.note: They face the same mandate and compliance costs as large firms despite the modest 15-employee threshold, though a 56-hour annual cap, no payout at separation, and credit for existing policies soften the burden.

Paid time off makes preventive and early care feasible for workers who currently skip it, shifting some demand from emergency rooms toward routine care, which the bill's findings say lowers overall costs.
